title: Inquest begins into police shooting of 18-year-old
subtitle: The family of Alwy Al-Nadhir, 18, is looking for answers into the killing of the teen by police in Riverdale Park as he attempted a holdup robbery.
article: An enlarged photo of a bloodied gunshot wound to the neck elicited a quiet moan from the victim's family but silence from the dead man's intended robbery victim, as an inquest began Monday into the police shooting of Alwy Al-Nadhir.
Al-Nadhir, 18, died at St. Michael's Hospital after a single police bullet entered his neck, passed through his left lung and exited through his back.

An investigation by the province's special investigations unit cleared police of wrongdoing in the case. But an inquest was called to examine the events surrounding his death and make recommendations for preventing similar deaths.

Al-Nadhir, a Grade 12 student at Central Tech, had had previous "brushes with the law" including an assault charge, and was on a peace bond at the time of the incident, Coroner's counsel Rebecca Edwards told the court before Dr. David Evans.

"Freeze. Drop it. Toronto police." Those were words robbery victim Natheeson Gobalasundaranathan, 25, testified that he heard the fateful evening of Halloween 2007. The arrival of police surprised two suspects who were in the act of trying to rob him and two friends at gunpoint at about 9:30 p.m., outside the pool entrance at Riverdale Park.

Gobalasundaranathan said he and his friend threw their hands up. He shouted out his innocence, just seconds after they'd been told to put up their hands and face the wall by two young men who had demanded their valuables. He had only a Metropass, due to expire that day, and a gold chain.
One of the assailants dropped his weapon, later discovered to be a pellet gun, and fell to the ground, with one police officer keeping his gun on him.

Gobalasundaranathan saw the second assailant, Al-Nadhir, run. He had taken only about three steps. "After a few seconds I hear a gunshot," Gobalasundaranathan told the court. Then he heard a second officer call out: "Talk to me, talk to me."
Although he never actually saw a weapon in Al-Nadhir's hands, Gobalasundaranathan saw him tugging at something in his pocket, which made him believe Al-Nadhir had a weapon, too.
He was relieved when police arrived. "I was so surprised. It never happens like this," said a grateful Gobalasundaranathan.
The first day of testimony was tough for Al-Nadhir's family.
"We just want to know the truth," his sister, Basma Al-Nadhir, 15, said outside court. "Just to see justice served," added her 16-year-old sister, Fatma Al-Nadhir.
